Airbnb’s 15.5% host-only fee, in numbers a payout statement already has.

Through 2025 and into 2026 Airbnb moved most hosts off the split-fee model — host about 3%, guest about 14% at checkout — onto a single host-only service fee of about 15.5% of the booking subtotal. Guests no longer see a separate Airbnb service fee. The platform’s take did not disappear; it moved onto the host’s side of the line.

Open the free payout calculator

What the fee applies to

The host service fee is a percentage of the booking subtotal: nightly rate × nights, plus cleaning and other mandatory host fees. Occupancy tax and a refundable security deposit are usually excluded. Payment processing is bundled into that percentage on Airbnb; it is a separate line on Vrbo.

Why “just add 15.5%” is the wrong raise

The fee is taken from the new listed subtotal, not the old one. If you used to keep 97% of $545 ($528.65) and you now keep 84.5%, the list that restores the old deposit is $545 × 0.97 ÷ 0.845 ≈ $626, a 14.8% raise — not 15.5%. Guests used to pay a ~14% service fee on top of $545. After you raise the list they often pay a similar all-in total with no separate service fee. That is arithmetic, not a pricing strategy.

What this page will not do

It will not tell you to leave Airbnb, to match a neighbour’s rate, or that 15.5% is the figure on your statement. Markets, professional-host rules, and VAT change the percentage. Replace the starting rate in the calculator with the one on your payout. Nothing you type is uploaded.

airbnb-vs-vrbo-host-fees.html.text:
← Back to the calculator

Airbnb vs Vrbo host fees are not two percentages of the same stay.

A blog that says “Airbnb takes 15.5%, Vrbo takes 8%” is flattening two different fee shapes. Airbnb’s host-only service fee is one percentage of the booking subtotal (nights + cleaning + extras), with processing bundled. Vrbo’s pay-per-booking model is a 5% commission on that same subtotal plus a 3% payment-processing fee on the guest payment, which usually includes occupancy tax and a security deposit. Those two threes are not on the same base.

Compare both on your own stay

On fees alone, Vrbo is usually cheaper in 2026

For a $225 × 2-night stay with a $95 cleaning fee, $200 deposit, and 10% tax, Airbnb host-only keeps about $84.50 of the $545 subtotal. Vrbo keeps about $27 in commission and about $24 in processing on the wider guest payment. The host’s per-stay gap is real. It is also incomplete: Airbnb may still deliver more booked nights. The calculator asks for marketplace bookings per year and, for a direct site, the share of those nights you would keep.

Direct booking is not “2.9% plus a website”

Card processing and a $29/month site look cheapest on a single reservation. They lose if the occupancy haircut is large. The useful number is the break-even: how many direct stays you need, after processing and the site cost, to match the best marketplace’s annual payout. If that figure is 80% of the nights Airbnb already sends, going direct is a demand problem, not a fee problem.

Vrbo’s annual subscription

Some existing hosts can still renew a subscription that drops the 5% commission and leaves the 3% processing. New hosts generally cannot join it. Treat it as a row you turn off unless you actually pay it. Spread the annual invoice over the bookings it carries — a $599 plan on four stays is not the same product as a $599 plan on forty.

No warranty. This is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it is not a quote from Airbnb or Vrbo. Starting rates are 2026 ballparks. Verify against your own statements. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Common questions

How much does Airbnb take from hosts in 2026?

Most hosts now pay a single host-only service fee of about 15.5% of the booking subtotal (nights plus cleaning and other mandatory fees). Guests no longer pay a separate Airbnb service fee at checkout. The older split-fee model — host ~3%, guest ~14% — is being retired. Replace the starting rate with the percentage on your own payout statement; this page only does the arithmetic.

Is Vrbo cheaper for hosts than Airbnb?

On fees alone, usually yes in 2026. Vrbo’s pay-per-booking model is typically 5% commission on the rental plus 3% payment processing on the guest payment, which includes tax and deposits. Airbnb’s host-only fee is about 15.5% of the subtotal. That gap can reverse if Airbnb’s demand keeps more nights booked, which is why this calculator also asks how many bookings you actually get and how many you would keep going direct.

How much should I raise my Airbnb rate after the 15.5% host-only fee?

To keep the same payout you had under a 3% host fee, the listed subtotal has to rise by about 14.8%, because 15.5% is taken from the new list price, not the old one. Guests used to pay a ~14% service fee on top; after you raise the list they often pay a similar all-in total with no separate service fee. Enter your own old and new rates above — the restore figure is arithmetic on those rates, not advice.

How many direct bookings do I need to break even with Airbnb or Vrbo fees?

More than the fee gap alone suggests. At the default stay ($225 × 2 nights, $545 subtotal, 36 marketplace bookings a year), the best available channel is Vrbo’s annual subscription at $18,158 a year — and direct booking needs about 35 stays a year, roughly 97% of those 36, to match it once card processing and the $29/month site cost are counted. A per-stay fee that looks small on paper can still make direct the losing channel if it costs you nearly as many bookings as it saves in fees. The break-even panel recomputes this from your own occupancy-kept percentage the moment you change it — it is not a fixed rule of thumb.

This calculator vs. Airbnb's own "Estimate your earnings" tool

Airbnb publishes a free Estimate your earnings tool for people considering listing a property: type an address and a few details, and it predicts a nightly price and monthly income on Airbnb. It is forward-looking and single-channel — a forecast for a listing that may not exist yet, already netting out Airbnb's own fee, with no way to add a Vrbo or direct-booking leg and no field for a stay you have already booked or priced.

That makes Airbnb's tool the right choice for "what might this property earn on Airbnb" before you list. This calculator answers a different question: for a stay you already have real numbers for, which channel actually pays the most — Airbnb, Vrbo, or direct — and what it would take to do better.

How many occupied nights can I afford to lose by going direct and still come out ahead? This calculator's direct-booking break-even.
What does Vrbo's pay-per-booking or legacy annual plan pay on the same stay? This calculator — Airbnb's tool has no Vrbo leg at all.

This tool needs no Airbnb account and no live listing: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your numbers stay on your device — nothing is uploaded anywhere, and a shareable link carries your inputs after the # in the URL rather than on a server.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Airbnb's Estimate Your Earnings tool?

Both, for different questions. Airbnb's own estimator, free on airbnb.com, predicts a nightly price and monthly income for a property you have not listed yet, on Airbnb only, already netting out their fee. This calculator instead takes a stay you already have numbers for — nightly rate, nights, cleaning fee, occupancy tax, deposit — and runs it through Airbnb's 15.5% host-only fee, the retired 3% split, Vrbo's pay-per-booking and legacy annual plans, and direct booking, side by side, plus the listed-price raise needed to restore an old 3% payout and the occupancy you can afford to lose going direct. Airbnb's tool cannot do any of that: it has no Vrbo or direct-booking leg and no way to enter an actual booked stay.

Does Airbnb's estimator account for Vrbo or direct booking?

No. It is single-channel by design — it forecasts what Airbnb itself would pay for a listing on Airbnb. It has no field for a Vrbo commission, Vrbo's annual subscription, or a direct-booking site's processing fee, so it cannot answer which channel actually pays best on a given stay.

vs-tracking-payouts-in-a-spreadsheet.htm.text:
← Airbnb/Vrbo host payout calculator

This calculator vs. tracking payouts in a spreadsheet

A host who compares more than one channel usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a cell for Airbnb's host-only fee, one for Vrbo's commission, another for Vrbo's processing rate, and a new tab whenever a rate changes or a booking count needs re-checking. Each formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping five channels' worth of them straight — especially the two Vrbo plans, which are not on the same fee base — is the part that gets skipped.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs: Airbnb's host-only fee against the subtotal, the retired split against the same subtotal, Vrbo's 5% commission plus 3% processing on the guest's payment (tax and deposit included), Vrbo's annual subscription with its flat fee divided by the bookings it actually covers, and direct booking's card processing weighed against the bookings you would keep after leaving the marketplace. Building it means pulling each rate from a different payout statement or fee page, typing the right one into the right cell, and remembering that Vrbo's two percentages are not on the same base before comparing them.

This calculator keeps all five channels wired to the same stay, so a nightly-rate change, a tax-rate correction, or Airbnb's next fee migration updates every channel's payout, guest total, and annual figure at once instead of in whichever cells someone remembers to touch. The restore-payout figure and the direct-booking break-even are computed the same way, from the same inputs, rather than derived by hand each time the question comes up.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which channel actually pays the most for this stay, once occupancy is counted?This calculator's annual-payout column — see below.
Are Vrbo's pay-per-booking and annual-subscription plans on the same fee base?No. This calculator prices each against its own base rather than one flat percentage.
What do I need to list at under the 15.5% host-only fee to keep my old 3% payout?This calculator's restore-payout figure — see below.
My situation has a wrinkle this calculator doesn't model (a multi-property portfolio, dynamic nightly pricing).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No, for either approach — a spreadsheet file stays wherever you saved it, and this calculator runs entirely in your browser.

One stay, five channels, a spreadsheet has to get the base right on each

Using this calculator's own worked example: a $220 nightly rate for 4 nights plus a $120 cleaning fee, a $1,000.00 subtotal, 8% occupancy tax, and 40 bookings a year on the marketplace.

ChannelPayout / stayGuest paysEffective host feeAnnual payout
Airbnb (host-only)$845.00$1,080.0015.5%$33,800.00
Airbnb (legacy split)$970.00$1,221.003%$38,800.00
Vrbo (pay-per-booking)$917.60$1,180.008.2%$36,704.00
Vrbo (annual subscription)$952.63$1,180.004.7%$38,105.00
Direct booking$958.27$1,080.004.2%$26,831.60

Direct booking's own payout per stay after its site cost, $958.27, is the highest of the four channels a host can actually choose today — only the retired split, a reference row almost no host can still select, pays more per stay at $970.00. A spreadsheet with a row for per-stay payout alone would call direct booking the winner among the real options. It is not: direct only keeps 28 of the host's 40 marketplace bookings a year, a 70% occupancy rate entered as an input, and once that trade is priced in, direct's annual payout is $26,831.60 — the lowest of the five, $11,273.40 below Vrbo's annual subscription. The break-even panel says exactly how tight that margin is: direct needs about 39.6 bookings a year, roughly 99% of the 40 the host already gets on the marketplace, before the occupancy trade stops costing more than the fees it avoids.

The reference row (Airbnb's retired split) is shown for comparison only; most hosts can no longer choose it. To keep that row's $970.00 payout under the 15.5% host-only fee, the listed subtotal has to rise from $1,000.00 to $1,147.93 — a 14.8% raise — and the guest's all-in total rises by only $6.93, from $1,221.00 to $1,227.93. Run your own stay through the calculator to see where it falls.

A spreadsheet is not wrong about the arithmetic — every number above is arithmetic a spreadsheet can do. What it does not do on its own is keep Vrbo's two fee bases apart, re-derive the occupancy break-even each time a booking count changes, or notice that the channel winning the per-stay row is losing the annual one. This calculator does not know your market's demand or your own booking history; it replaces the bookkeeping a spreadsheet has to be told to do every time.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. Every formula this calculator runs — Airbnb's host-only fee, the retired split, Vrbo's pay-per-booking commission and processing, Vrbo's annual subscription amortized over the bookings it covers, and direct booking's processing and site cost — is ordinary arithmetic. Getting it right means keeping straight that Vrbo's 5% commission and 3% processing are not on the same base (processing runs on the guest's total including tax and deposit, the commission does not), that the subscription plan's $499–699 has to be divided by how many stays it actually carries before it can be compared to a percentage, and that a cheaper per-stay fee on paper can still lose on paper once you weight it by the bookings you would actually keep.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Keep five channels' formulas in sync when a rate changes, and recompute the direct-booking break-even the moment you change how many bookings you would actually keep going direct. Airbnb's 2026 migration from a 3% host fee to a 15.5% host-only fee changed the number in one cell of a spreadsheet built before it; the five other cells that depend on it — the guest-paid total, the effective fee, the restore-payout figure — only update if someone remembers to touch them too. This calculator recomputes all of it the moment one input changes, and turns the occupancy trade-off in going direct into one figure instead of a rule of thumb.

Why doesn't the channel with the highest per-stay payout also win the year?

Because a spreadsheet that only has a row for the per-stay number is answering a different question than the one that decides where to list. On this calculator's own worked example, direct booking's payout after its site cost, $958.27, is the highest of the four channels a host can actually choose today — only the retired split, a reference row almost no host can still select, pays more per stay at $970.00. But direct only keeps 28 of the host's 40 marketplace bookings a year, and once that 70% occupancy is priced in, its annual payout is $26,831.60: the lowest of the five, $11,273.40 below Vrbo's annual subscription. The per-stay number and the annual number rank the real channels in a different order, and a spreadsheet has to compute both to notice.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a shape this calculator's inputs cannot represent — a multi-property portfolio with different rates per listing, dynamic pricing that changes the nightly rate booking to booking, or a channel running a promotional commission this tool's fields cannot capture. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one stay moving through the fee, tax, and occupancy questions most hosts actually face.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your numbers after the # in the URL rather than sending them to a server, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day — never your rates, occupancy, or address.

This page names no vendor as a competitor — it compares against the generic method of tracking payouts across channels in a spreadsheet, not a competing calculator or service.
